evidence: In operators/compositions/__init__.py, ExplicitStack.Layer_Outputs (One_Layer) computes kernel_output = layer.kernel.Forward(...) and local_output = layer.local_linear.Forward(...), then activated = Activated(..., local_output + kernel_output), and adds the input back when layer.residual is set (activated = activated + entering). That is sigma(W z + K z) + z: the parent FNO layer with a residual added. In operators/factorized_fourier/__init__.py, Explicit_Layers builds Layer(kernel=SpectralKernel(mode_mixing='separable'), local_linear=PointwiseLift(64,64), residual=True). No two-layer feedforward follows the spectral convolution. The F-FNO paper's layer, recalled from knowledge because the web is off-limits, is z + sigma(W2 sigma(W1 K(z) + b1) + b2): no local linear bypass inside the activation, a two-layer feedforward after K, and the residual after the nonlinearity. The kernel itself does match F-FNO in effect. It adds per-axis weights over a 3-D FFT box (SEPARABLE_SUBSCRIPTS) with 19 kept modes on a 40-point axis, which covers essentially the whole spectrum and so matches the paper's sum of per-axis 1-D transforms. IMPLEMENTATION.md describes the build ('beside a PointwiseLift(64, 64) local linear term, residual, GELU') but records no difference from the paper's layer. test-suite.md I.1 and the manifest cite only F-FNO. The name is defensible for the kernel, and the claim that the layer differs without any record is accurate.

In operators/metrics/__init__.py, Gap_Edge_Energies computes 'supported = carried >= support_fraction * peak; occupied_side = energies[supported & (energies <= gap_reference)]; empty_side = energies[supported & (energies >= gap_reference)]', with gap_reference defaulting to 0.0. operators/deep_operator_network/report.py:732 calls 'Gap_Edge_Error(predicted_curve, truth_curve, self.energy_grid)' without a reference, on a grid aligned so that 0 is the valence-band maximum. The read-out's 'empty side' therefore starts at the first grid point at or above the valence-band maximum, inside the smeared valence edge. I recomputed this on the 248 test truths (State_Density_Examples, strain_to_states, role test; data loading only). The grid points near 0 are [-0.04, 0.02, 0.08]. With the reference at the valence-band maximum, the conduction-side edge is 0.02 for every run (unique values [0.02]) and the valence-side edge is -0.82 or -0.04. Those are the first grid points on each side, not band edges. With the reference at mid-gap (valence-band maximum + occupancy-walk gap / 2), the same read-out gives gaps from 0.06 to 5.28 eV (median 3.66), against occupancy-walk gaps of 0.44 to 5.77 eV (median 4.07), with correlation r = 0.9983. So the degeneracy comes from the reference argument the report passes. It is not a limit of the support-edge metric, and smearing alone does not explain it. The printed gap_edge_error values (floors 0.000000, member 1.9125) do not measure band-edge placement. The report's 'that is the metric's own limit' and the page's 'an artifact of the smearing on this window' give the wrong cause.

Quote (IMPLEMENTATION.md): 'predicting exactly zero in standardized space already *is* the training-mean field, so every unit of gradient that moves the prediction away from zero is now working on the lattice-dependent deviation the gate actually measures'. Right part: with targets (t-mu)/sigma (Perovskite_Gate_Example), zero is the training-mean field, and the residual the loss sees is the deviation from that mean. Wrong part: the standardized MSE is sum_v (p_v-t_v)^2/sigma_v^2, a per-voxel 1/sigma^2 reweighting. The gate's relative L2 (operators.metrics.Relative_L2 on the raw density) weights every voxel's error equally. Measured on the gate's own data (scratch check021.py: train stats from Perovskite_Gate_Training_Examples, 80 train runs; mean-field residual on the 25 Angle_Stratum_Examples('evaluation',0) runs, 262144 voxels): 'top 1% highest-spread voxels: share of raw (gate) squared deviation = 0.209; share of standardized-loss mass = 0.009'; 'top 5%: 0.537 vs 0.045'; 'top 10%: 0.711 vs 0.092'. A unit raw error at a top-1% voxel weighs about 0.005 of the same error at a median voxel. So the loss works on the same deviation field, but heavily down-weights the high-variance voxels that carry most of the gate's measured error, as the claim says. 'the deviation the gate actually measures' is therefore misleading as a description of the loss. The claim's flat 'does not work on the deviation' overstates it: the deviation is the same field, only the weighting differs.

evidence: IMPLEMENTATION.md:47 says normalizing K and V rather than Q and K 'is what makes the map softmax-free'. In the code (__init__.py GalerkinAttentionKernel.Forward), the map is softmax-free simply because no softmax is applied: key_value = einsum('hdn,hen->hde', K~, V~), then attended = einsum('hde,hdm->hem', key_value, Q)/N. Which pair gets normalized only decides between the two variants in Cao 2021. Galerkin-type normalizes K and V, Q(K~^T V~)/n. Fourier-type normalizes Q and K, (Q~K~^T)V/n, and it is also softmax-free. What makes the cost linear in N is the order of association (K^T V first), not the normalization. The code matches the Galerkin variant, so the code is right and only the explanation is wrong.

operators/residual_correction/__init__.py, ProjectionBackbone.Forward_Correction: docstring 'the raw predicted correction, a leading batch axis carrying each pair's own field', but the body ends with '# ... each pair losing only its own mean, exactly the zero-mean law applied one field at a time' / 'return raw_correction - Channel_Means(raw_correction)'. Channel_Means (operators/wrappers) takes each row's mean over its voxels, so the return value is the zero-mean (conserved) correction. The wrapper's own docstring says so: ResidualCorrection.Forward_Correction is documented as 'the conserved correction alone' and just calls the backbone. ProjectionBackbone.__call__, by contrast, does return the raw readout output (Conserving removes the mean there), so the docstring describes a different path from the one it sits on.

operators/tests/test_residual_correction.py, Lifted_Loss: docstring 'a coefficient-regression loss closed over one engine's own lifted constants'; the body computes 'predicted = member.Forward_Correction(full_lifted, cheap_coefficients)', 'residuals = predicted - true_correction', 'return (residuals * residuals).mean()'. Every call site passes the full flattened correction fields as true_correction (e.g. 'Lifted_Loss(member, engine, cheap_coefficients, correction_fields)'), and Forward_Correction returns voxel fields. So the loss is the mean squared error over every voxel of the correction field, not a regression on coefficients. It only mislabels a test helper, so S5.

Code: ProjectionBackbone builds PointwiseStandardizedExpansion(Zero_Anchored(correction_basis), grid, zeros, voxel_scale). That readout (operators/readouts) computes 'standardized = branch_vector @ basis_modes + basis_mean + lifted["output_bias"]; return standardized * voxel_scale + voxel_mean'. The modes come from Gram_Pod on the raw training corrections (mean-centered POD), so the reachable outputs are span{mode_k*voxel_scale, voxel_scale} minus each pair's mean, with the basis mean and voxel mean set to zero. Recomputed (ceiling2.py/ceiling3.py), giving every test pair its own free coefficients and its own bias, which is a lower bound on the member's error: the test ceiling has unit-median median 0.002077 (run-level median 0.002082, range 0.00194-0.00223). report.md's member median is 0.002079, and the proper rank-32 ceiling of the same basis is 0.0000022. The training-loss floor of this readout is 3.2579e-06 (mean squared residual). The manifests' final losses are 3.2879e-06 (stage 0), 3.2719e-06 (stage 1) and 3.2700e-06 (stage 2), starting from 9.1e-05, so training plateaued at the floor. In the ceiling residual of each test pair, the share of energy along the block's one mean residual field has median 0.9915 (minimum 0.9156; train 0.978): one fixed field carries nearly all the error. The coefficients this readout needs reach |1303.7| (QR least squares). The figure cache inspection.npz has backbone.readout.last_coefficients max |1290.63| for one test pair, while correction_basis_singular_values max is 3.1839. The block's mean correction field has norm 2.432 against a typical correction norm of 2.443, so the zero-anchored readout throws away almost the whole signal and has to rebuild it from mode*scale products. Consequence: report.md's 'the network adds nothing over linear regression' (member 406x the ridge) is a reading of this readout's ceiling, not of what the branch can learn. The canon-bar pass (0.002079 <= 0.005565) still stands.

Resolution_Axis feeds the operator Carried_On_Grid(probe.input_function, training_shape) and asks for output at evaluation_shape. The null truncates the truth itself. When the truth's above-band content is a function of the in-band input, an operator can beat the null. My own test (scratch null_beatable.py) uses invariance.Spectral_Truncation_Resample on a 12^3 grid with a 6^3 training shape: the input is band-limited at |k|<=1 and the truth is input**3, which has modes up to |k|=3. An 'operator' that upsamples the coarse input and cubes it pointwise gives model error 1.59e-15 against null error 0.1348, skill 0.99999999999999. So the null is a reference level, not a floor. The same claim is repeated: test_invariance.py docstring 'an operator handed only the coarse input cannot beat carrying the coarse truth back up' and comment '# the null is the floor of the axis'; test-suite.md 9.5(a) 'Null: trigonometric upsampling of the coarse truth = the irreducible truncation floor'. Skill_Against_Null computes 1 - err/null with no clipping at zero, so the arithmetic is unaffected; only the description is wrong.
